segments.heading: Segment 1
segments.text:
Baghdad had no stone. No timber. No harbor. No mine. Within fifty years of the first brick, it was the richest city on Earth. That is not luck. Nobody gets lucky for five hundred years.

Picture the river docks at dawn, so packed with grain barges you could cross the water without touching it.
Picture a merchant handing over a slip of paper in Baghdad and collecting hard silver for it two thousand miles away.
Picture a translator paid, so the story goes, in gold that weighed as much as the book he had just finished.

Plenty of cities sat on a crossroads. Almost none of them worked out how to build the tollbooth. Baghdad did, and then it did something harder. It kept it running for half a millennium.

So here is what you are going to see. First, every mechanism that turned a muddy bend in a river into the financial center of the old world.
The canals, the coins, the contracts, the paper. Then the part almost nobody tells you. How those same mechanisms were taken apart, slowly, quietly, by the very people paid to protect them.

Five centuries to build. Two weeks to end. If you want to keep watching empires get built and taken apart like this, subscribing is how you stay for the rest of the Empire Economics series.
Now, let us go back to the beginning.

Because before any of it, one man had to make a decision that could have destroyed his dynasty.

<#1#>

Every empire eventually makes one decision that quietly settles everything that comes after it. The Abbasids made theirs in the year seven hundred and sixty two.

Twelve years before that, they had pulled down the Umayyad caliphate and inherited an empire that ran from Spain to the edge of India. What they also inherited was a capital in the wrong place.
Damascus looked west, out over the Mediterranean, toward a Roman world that had stopped being the center of anything. The wealth had drifted east.
It was sitting in the river valleys and the caravan towns further east. Damascus could not reach any of it without going the long way round.

Al Mansur did not try to fix the old capital. He abandoned it.
He went looking for ground where the Tigris and the Euphrates come closest to each other, and he built on the gap between them.

Understand what that site actually was. Rivers carried freight in bulk. Roads carried it in small loads at high cost. This one point touched both.
The Tigris ran down to the Gulf, and the Gulf opened onto India and, eventually, China. The Euphrates ran up toward Syria and the Mediterranean. The land routes east went to Persia and Central Asia.
He was not choosing a place to live. He was choosing a junction.

And here is the part that usually gets left out. The dynasty was twelve years old. Twelve.
It still had rivals with armies, provinces that had not decided anything yet, and a family tree full of people who thought the job should have gone to them.
Al Mansur took the treasury of a state that could still have collapsed, and he spent it on empty ground.

What went up was a perfect circle, about a mile and a half across, wrapped in three rings of wall.
Four gates, each one aimed at a road that was already carrying trade before the city existed. Something like a hundred thousand people worked on it.
Brickmakers, surveyors, water engineers, laborers hauling clay out of the riverbank.

The cost is where the sources start arguing with each other.
The city's own chronicler, al Khatib al Baghdadi, and the geographer al Yaqubi hand down figures that range from roughly five million dirhams to something near eighteen million, and nobody today can settle it.
But take the smallest number on the table. A laborer on that site earned one or two dirhams a month. Five million dirhams buys you more than three million months of that work.
Spread across a hundred thousand men, that is nearly three years of an entire workforce, paid for out of a treasury that had no guarantee of existing the following spring.

It worked. Within a generation the gamble looked obvious, the way successful gambles always do afterward. But the bill for it never arrived all at once.

But a capital investment only pays off if it survives its first bad harvest. And Baghdad grew absolutely nothing.

<#1#>

So how do you feed a city that produces no food at all?

Baghdad sat on sand and clay. Nothing edible grew inside the walls, and nothing edible grew for miles around them unless somebody made it.
The answer was sitting just south of the city, in the flat alluvial country between the two rivers that the Arabs called the Sawad, the black land, named for how dark the soil went when it was wet.

That soil could produce two harvests a year. It could also produce nothing at all. The difference was entirely mechanical. Water had to be lifted out of the rivers by wheels turning day and night.
It had to be moved through cut channels and underground conduits.
It had to be let in and shut off by gates, in the right week, in the right volume, because too little water starved the crop and too much of it left salt behind in the soil.

Two of those channels deserve their names said out loud. The Isa canal and the Sarsar canal did not just irrigate.
They cut clean across from the Euphrates to the Tigris, which meant a barge loaded in the west could float all the way to the Baghdad docks without a single sack being lifted off and put down again.
Every time cargo changes hands it costs money and some of it goes missing. Those canals removed the handling. Grain arrived cheaper than it had any right to be.

Now the state had to take its cut without killing the thing it was taxing. That job belonged to a bureau called the Diwan al Kharaj.
Land tax, assessed on what a field could actually yield rather than a flat demand. A trade duty of ten percent on goods moving through. A tax on non Muslim subjects.
And zakat, the obligatory alms every Muslim owed. Four separate streams, recorded, audited, and argued over by professional clerks who wrote manuals about how to do it properly.
One of them, a treasury official named Qudama ibn Jafar, quite literally wrote the book on how to tax a province.

And then there were the granaries. The state held grain in reserve across several years, which is a boring sentence describing an extraordinary capability.
When a harvest failed and prices started to climb, the reserves were released into the market until the price came back down.
Hoarding to drive prices up was treated as a crime, not a clever trade. A medieval city with no famine panic is not a city that got lucky with the weather.
It is a city with a functioning food policy.

How many people this fed is genuinely disputed. You will hear the figure of one million, and you will also hear serious historians call that far too high.
What is not disputed is that Baghdad was, for a while, the largest city on the planet, and that every mouth in it depended on the same narrow strip of engineered ground. Which is worth holding onto.
The whole thing stood on one piece of land, and that land only stayed alive as long as somebody dredged the channels every year.

Once the granaries were full, something else could arrive. Not grain. People.

<#1#>

Somewhere around the year eight hundred and seventy, a geographer working for the Abbasid postal service wrote down something strange.
There were merchants, he said, who travelled from the land of the Franks all the way to China, and back. And every one of their routes passed through the same place.

His name was Ibn Khurradadhbih, and he called these traders the Radhanites. He does not give us a single one of them by name.
What he gives us is the route, written down by a man whose job was knowing every road in the empire. They spoke Arabic, Persian, Greek, Frankish and more.
They ran from the coast of southern France, through Egypt, down the Red Sea, across to India, and on to China. Not as an adventure. As a business, repeated, in both directions.

So when people say Baghdad connected east and west, that undersells it and gets the geography slightly wrong.
What passed through Baghdad was traffic from one end of Eurasia to the other, plus everything the Indian Ocean and the African coast could put on a boat.
And most of it ended up in one district, on the west bank, called Karkh.

Silk and porcelain out of China. Pepper and cinnamon out of India. Teak and gemstones from the far side of the Bay of Bengal. Horses and furs down from the steppe. Gold and ivory up from Africa.
Amber from the Baltic, and Frankish swords good enough that Muslim merchants bought them to fight Frankish armies with.

None of this was thrown together. Karkh was zoned, trade by trade. Textiles sat under covered arcades where the light was good and the goods stayed dry.
Tanners and coppersmiths, the loud trades and the ones that stank, were pushed out to the edges. Booksellers clustered next to the scholars.
Walk through any modern trade fair and you will see the same idea, twelve hundred years later.

But zoning is the easy part. Here is the hard problem. A man from Cordoba and a man from Bukhara have never met, share no law court, and will probably never see each other again.
Why would either of them trust a set of scales, or a sack that is supposed to be full, or a coin that is supposed to be silver?

Because someone was checking. The office was called the hisba, and the official who ran it walked the market. He tested weights against the standard. He assayed metal for purity. He inspected food.
He broke up attempts to corner a supply. He could fine you, shut you down, or have you paraded through the street you had cheated in.

That is the thing worth taking away from this. A market is not what happens when you leave people alone in a square.
A market is what happens when a stranger can be held to account. Baghdad built that, and the whole world came to use it.

And that raises a problem nobody in Europe had solved yet. How does a man from Cordoba pay a man from Bukhara without carrying a fortune in silver across four thousand miles of bandit country?

<#1#>

There is a story we like to tell about where modern finance was born. Renaissance Italy. Florentine bankers. It is a good story. It is also about four hundred years late.

Start with the money itself. Baghdad ran three metals at once. A gold dinar for large sums, weighing a shade over four grams, struck at high purity. A silver dirham for ordinary trade. Copper for the man buying bread.
Three tiers, so that a shipment of silk and a loaf could be priced in the same system without anybody carrying a bag of gold dust around.

And the mints were held to it. Weight and purity were checked and defended, because a caliph who quietly shaved the silver content of his own coinage was not being clever.
He was destroying the one thing that made the currency worth holding beyond his own borders. Which brings us to the best evidence in this entire video, and it was dug up in Sweden.

On the island of Gotland, a farmer's field gave up the largest Viking silver hoard ever found.
Inside it, thousands of coins, and a great many of them Abbasid dirhams that had travelled from the mints of the caliphate up the Russian rivers into the Baltic. Nobody sent those coins as tribute. Nobody was forced to take them.
Traders at the far northern edge of the known world simply preferred a currency they could rely on over one they could not.
That is what a reserve currency looks like before anyone has invented the phrase.

Now back to the merchant with the payment problem. He does not carry the silver.
He deposits it in Baghdad and receives a written order to pay, called a sakk, which the holder can present somewhere else.
For longer distances there was the suftaja, a letter of credit honoured by a correspondent in another city. Follow one of those letters for a moment.
A trader hands his silver over a counter in Karkh, folds the receipt into his coat, and rides out with an empty saddlebag.
Weeks later, a thousand miles east, he presents that same slip of paper and walks away with local coin. The silver never made the journey. Only the promise did.
And a promise, unlike a mule train, cannot be ambushed on the road.
Handling all of this was a profession, the jahbadh, part banker and part money changer, who knew what a Byzantine coin was worth in Persian silver on a Tuesday.
And to fund the voyage itself there was the mudaraba, where one party puts up the capital, the other does the travelling, they split the profit on agreed terms, and the investor can lose the stake but never more than the stake.

Read that last one again. Capital on one side, labour on the other, profit shared, liability capped. That is a limited liability partnership, running in the ninth century, four hundred years before Florence.

And these ideas did not stay in Baghdad. They came to us inside our own vocabulary. The word cheque comes from sakk. Algebra comes from al jabr, the title of a book written in Baghdad.
Algorithm is not a concept, it is a person, a mangled Latin version of the name al Khwarizmi. Tariff most likely comes from the Arabic for a notification of charges. Magazine comes from makhzan, a storehouse.
Arsenal comes from the Arabic for a place of manufacture. Admiral comes from amir, commander. Every time you write a cheque, you are using a word Baghdad invented, for a thing Baghdad invented.

If that just rearranged something in your head, a like genuinely helps this reach people who still think it started in Florence. Now, the strangest part is still ahead.

Because all of this ran on something that had to be invented first. Not a coin. Not a contract. A surface.

<#1#>

The most valuable thing Baghdad ever manufactured weighed almost nothing, and cost almost nothing. It was a sheet of paper.

Before paper, writing something down left you two options. Parchment, which is animal skin, and which is expensive because you have to kill the animal.
Or papyrus, which is cheaper but cracks, and which only Egypt could supply. Both of them put a hard ceiling on how much a society could afford to record. Paper broke that ceiling.
Rag pulp, water, a mould, and a drying wall. Baghdad built mills that turned it out in volume.

Where the technique came from is a good story with a question mark on it.
The usual version says Chinese prisoners taken at a battle near the Talas river, in the year seven hundred and fifty one, gave up the secret. It is repeated everywhere.
It is also doubted by serious historians of paper, who point out the timeline does not quite fit and the craft may have arrived by ordinary trade instead.
Either way, by the end of that century Baghdad was making paper at industrial scale.

And a state that can suddenly afford to write things down starts behaving differently. Tax records get longer. Court rulings get archived.
And in Baghdad, the caliphs went one step further and funded knowledge the way you would fund a shipyard.
The House of Wisdom was a library, a translation bureau and a research institute in one building. Envoys were sent to Byzantium, to Syria, to Persia, with instructions to bring back manuscripts. Greek medicine, Indian mathematics, Persian astronomy. Bought, copied, argued with, corrected.

The translators were not clerks. They were the most sought after professionals in the empire.
The story told about the greatest of them, a physician and translator named Hunayn ibn Ishaq, is that the caliph paid him in gold matching the weight of the books he handed in. Whether that literally happened, we cannot verify.
Biographers wrote it down long afterwards. But you do not invent a legend like that about a profession nobody values.
Somewhere behind that story is a society that decided a translated book was worth its weight in metal.

And this paid. Not in prestige. In money. The number system that came up from India, worked through in Baghdad, made arithmetic something an ordinary clerk could do at speed.
Estates could be divided under inheritance law without a scholar being called in. Tax could be assessed across a province in a season instead of a year.
Better astronomical tables meant a captain in the Indian Ocean could find his position and get home. Agricultural manuals moved crops and irrigation methods from one province to another.
This is research and development, funded by the state, returning yield.

And once it was cheap to copy, knowledge stopped being something you had to be rich to touch.
Baghdad had a street given over entirely to booksellers and copying workshops, sitting right beside the scholars, which is the medieval version of a publishing industry. A man of modest means could own books.
That had not been true anywhere, for anyone, before.

This is the top of the curve. Everything from this point on is Baghdad spending what it just built. And the first bill came from a place nobody was watching.

<#1#>

Now keep that city in your head, at its absolute peak, and let one hundred years pass.
Because the Baghdad you just watched being assembled is about to start taking itself apart, one reasonable decision at a time.

Start with the army, because that is where the money goes. A professional soldier could draw something in the region of eighty dirhams a month.
Remember the men who built the walls, on one or two. One soldier cost what forty labourers cost.
Now multiply that by tens of thousands of men, and add the horses, the weapons, the frontier forts, and the Turkish regiments brought in precisely because they owed nothing to anyone in the provinces.

Here is the trap, and it is not a medieval trap. Defence is a fixed cost. It gets paid whether the year is good or bad, and it only ever goes up. Revenue is not fixed.
It rises and falls with the harvest, and with whether a province feels like paying this year. And the two are wired together backwards.
When trouble arrives, income drops and the cost of holding the empire together climbs, at the same time, for the same reason.

Watch what a state does when it is squeezed.
In the year eight hundred and thirty six, with the Turkish troops and the population of Baghdad at each other's throats, the caliph did not fix the problem. He moved out.
He built an entirely new capital upriver at Samarra and took the government with him. The figures for what that cost do not agree, so I will not pretend to one.
What is not in doubt is the shape of it. A treasury already stretched by soldiers paid for a second capital, so the soldiers would stop rioting in the first one.

It did not buy peace. Between eight hundred and sixty one and eight hundred and seventy, four caliphs were killed by their own commanders.
The men hired to protect the state had worked out that they were now the state.

And then comes the decision that actually killed Baghdad. It was made by people trying to be responsible. The treasury could not pay the commanders in coin. So it paid them in land.
Not ownership exactly, but the right to collect the taxes on a district and keep the proceeds. The arrangement is called iqta, and on paper it is elegant.
The army gets paid, the treasury gets relief, nobody has to move silver around.

Look at what it does to incentives. A salaried official had a career that lasted decades. Keeping the canals clear was in his interest, because his province had to still be producing in twenty years.
A commander holding a grant has no such horizon. He may lose it next season, or be reassigned, or die. His interest is to take as much out of that land as fast as possible.
So he floods the field for one more crop this year, and lets the salt it leaves behind become the next man's problem. Multiply that across a province, across thirty years.

Nobody dredges. Silt builds in the channels. Salt builds in the fields. The archaeologist Robert Adams later walked that ground and read the whole collapse straight off the buried canals and the ruined soil.
Yields fall, so the tax take falls, so there is less money for the canals, so the yields fall again. Nobody chose that. Everybody caused it.
And the merchants still came through, generation after generation, past canals a little shallower each time, into a city that was still magnificent and no longer being maintained.

By the time the horsemen appeared on the horizon, the thing they came to destroy had already been dying for four generations. They just finished it in two weeks.

<#1#>

On the tenth of February, twelve fifty eight, the gates open.

But hold that image, because the ending was arranged long before anyone rode up to the walls.

Go back three hundred years. In the year nine hundred and sixty nine, a rival dynasty takes Egypt and founds a new capital at Cairo. And they do something clever.
They make it cheaper and safer to run the India trade up the Red Sea than through the Gulf. Ships that would have unloaded for Baghdad start unloading for Cairo instead. Nobody fights a battle over this.
The route simply moves, the way water moves, and it does not come back out of politeness. Then Central Asia fragments, and the overland roads stop being safe to travel with a loaded caravan.
And a state running out of money does the one thing it must never do. It starts putting less silver in the coins.
Which works, briefly, and then stops working, because traders in Gotland and Bukhara can weigh metal. Trust was the product. It took two centuries to build and a generation to spend.

So when the Mongol army arrives under Hulagu Khan, it is not attacking the richest city on Earth.
It is attacking a capital that is still enormous, still full of books and scholars and markets, and financially hollow.

The siege lasts two weeks. The city surrenders. What happens next is usually told as a massacre, and it was one. The death toll is genuinely unknown.
The figure Hulagu himself gave in a letter to the king of France is enormous. Later writers pushed it higher. Modern historians think most of these numbers are impossible for a city that size.
The honest answer is that we are counting in the hundreds of thousands and cannot be more precise.

But the killing is not the part that decides the next seven hundred years. The Mongols broke the water system on purpose. Dykes cut. Control gates destroyed.
And this time there was no administration left to repair it, no treasury to fund the work, and nobody left who knew which channel mattered.
The Sawad, the black land that had fed the largest city on the planet, went to dust in some places and malarial marsh in others, and it stayed that way for centuries.

And then there is the loss nobody can put a number on.

The libraries burned. The House of Wisdom, the private collections, the copying workshops on the booksellers' street. Contemporary writers describe the Tigris running black with ink for days.
That image is almost certainly a symbol rather than a measurement, but it is what people reached for when they tried to say what had been done.

Yet the books are not the worst of it. Books can be rewritten. What died with the people was everything that had never been written down.
The engineer who knew which canal silts up first after a dry winter, and which month you have to open it. The potter who knew how long that kiln holds its heat.
The banker who knew which family in Aleppo honours a letter of credit and which one argues. None of that is in a book.
It lives in individual heads, it passes by standing next to somebody for ten years, and when those people are killed or marched off, it is gone in an afternoon.

That is why the city never came back. You can rebuild a wall. You cannot rebuild a network of people who all know things about each other.

If you want to know how long that shadow runs, look at the map today.
That same ground sits on some of the largest oil reserves on the planet, and it is not the centre of world commerce.
Because the wealth was never in the soil, or in the ground underneath it.
It was in the canals, the courts, the clerks, the credit, and the people who knew how all of it fitted together. A building goes up in a year.
That takes a century, and only if nothing interrupts.

What looks like nature is almost always engineering. And what looks like an inevitable fall is almost always a list of decisions that did not have to go that way.

If there is one word for what actually killed Baghdad, it is not the Mongols. Leave that word below. Maintenance.

And if this changed how you read the word decline, a like pushes it in front of the next person, the same way you found it.
Subscribe if you want to see what the next empire did with this exact lesson.

Here is the part that keeps bothering me. Three hundred years later, another empire inherits the same crossroads, the same routes, and the same problem. And this time they know exactly how Baghdad died.
They build a state designed specifically not to repeat it. Land held differently. Soldiers paid differently. Trade taxed differently. For three centuries, it works.

So why does that empire end up bankrupt anyway, with European banks collecting its taxes for it?

That one is sitting right there in front of you.
